t: For expenses necessary for the construction, acquisition, or conversion of vessels as authorized by law, including armor and armament thereof, plant equipment, appliances, and machine tools, and installation thereof in public or private plants; procurement of critical, long leadtime components and designs for vessels to be constructed or converted in the future; and expansion of public and private plants, including land necessary therefor, and such land, and interests therein, may be acquired and construction prosecuted thereon prior to approval of title by the Attorney General as required by section 355, Revised Statutes, as amended; $820,700,000, to remain available until expended: Provided, That none of the funds herein provided for the construction or conversion of any naval vessel to be constructed in shipyards in the United States shall be expended in foreign shipyards for the construction of major components of the hull or superstructure of such vessel: Provided further, That none of the funds herein provided shall be used for the construction of any naval vessel in foreign shipyards.

fable.w: This is an appropriation for naval shipbuilding with restrictions on spending in foreign shipyards. The tempting reading is that the Attorney General's title approval or the mention of private plants signals outside involvement, but the Attorney General is a federal official and private plants are only places where the work is done, not parties consulted on a federal decision. There is no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside entities, or right to sue.
fable.s: prior to approval of title by the Attorney General as required by section 355, Revised Statutes, as amended

qwen_block.w: This section is an appropriations provision that authorizes funding for the construction and acquisition of naval vessels and related infrastructure. It specifies where funds can and cannot be spent (e.g., prohibiting expenditure in foreign shipyards) but does not require consultation, coordination, or participation with any outside parties (such as the public, states, or private entities) in the decision-making process. The mention of 'private plants' refers to the location of work, not a participatory role in federal decisions.
qwen_block.s: For expenses necessary for the construction, acquisition, or conversion of vessels as authorized by law, including armor and armament thereof, plant equipment, appliances, and machine tools, and installation thereof in public or private plants; procurement of critical, long leadtime components and designs for vessels to be constructed or converted in the future; and expansion of public and private plants, including land necessary therefor, and such land, and interests therein, may be acquired and construction prosecuted thereon prior to approval of title by the Attorney General as required by section 355, Revised Statutes, as amended; $820,700,000, to remain available until expended: Provided, That none of the funds herein provided for the construction or conversion of any naval vessel to be constructed in shipyards in the United States shall be expended in foreign shipyards for the construction of major components of the hull or superstructure of such vessel: Provided further, That none of the funds herein provided shall be used for the construction of any naval vessel in foreign shipyards.

opus.w: This is an appropriation for building Navy vessels, with limits on spending in foreign shipyards. The only approval it mentions is title approval by the Attorney General, who is a federal official, and the provision even lets land be acquired before that approval. Because no state, company, expert, or member of the public takes part in any federal decision, this does not count as participation.
opus.s: such land, and interests therein, may be acquired and construction prosecuted thereon prior to approval of title by the Attorney General as required by section 355, Revised Statutes, as amended
opus.b: This is an appropriations provision for building and converting Navy vessels. One reading might look like participation: the reference to "approval of title by the Attorney General." That fails because the Attorney General is a federal official, so the step stays inside the government. The provision actually lets land be acquired before that approval anyway. The rest of the text sets funding amounts and restricts work in foreign shipyards. No outside party is consulted, and there is no hearing, comment period, advisory body, rulemaking, or right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: This section is an appropriations provision that authorizes the spending of funds for naval vessel construction and sets restrictions on where those funds can be used (e.g., prohibiting use in foreign shipyards). It does not require or recommend any consultation, coordination, or participation with outside parties (such as private shipyards, states, or the public) in the decision-making process. The mention of 'private plants' refers to the location of work, not a participatory role for the plant owners.
qwen_chat.s: For expenses necessary for the construction, acquisition, or conversion of vessels as authorized by law... $820,700,000, to remain available until expended: Provided, That none of the funds herein provided for the construction or conversion of any naval vessel to be constructed in shipyards in the United States shall be expended in foreign shipyards for the construction of major components of the hull or superstructure of such vessel: Provided further, That none of the funds herein provided shall be used for the construction of any naval vessel in foreign shipyards.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the mention of "private plants" and "private shipyards" implies coordination with private entities. However, the text only authorizes the expenditure of funds for construction *in* these plants or the acquisition of land; it does not mandate any consultation, advisory process, or public participation mechanism with the owners of these private facilities before the government makes its funding or construction decisions. The restrictions are purely on where the money can be spent (e.g., not in foreign shipyards), not on who must be consulted.
